# Introduction 
The purpose of this statistical report is to analyze the factors that may influence the dropout rate in public schools across different U.S. states. The dataset was obtained from official educational records across multiple U.S. states during the 2018–2019 academic year, including 1,200 school-level observations, and includes several school-level indicators such as funding per student, percentage of low-income students, percentage of minority students, average test scores, and the student–teacher ratio. In this project, the dropout rate (%) is considered the main dependent variable (Y).

Our goal is to understand how the dropout rate changes in relation to socioeconomic and academic factors (X variables). By identifying patterns within the data, this analysis may help schools and policymakers better understand the conditions that contribute to higher or lower dropout levels.

To achieve this, we apply descriptive statistics, visual exploration, and correlation analysis to summarize the characteristics of each variable and examine their relationships with the dropout rate. We also apply simple linear regression for each predictor separately, followed by a full multiple linear regression model that includes all predictors together. This approach helps us determine whether any of these factors significantly explain variation in dropout rate.


\newpage
#  Data Loading 


```{r Data Loading, echo=FALSE}
# Adjust path to your dataset location
data <- read.csv("education_inequality_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
df<-data
key_vars <- c(
  "funding_per_student_usd","percent_low_income","percent_minority",
  "avg_test_score_percent","dropout_rate_percent",
  "internet_access_percent","student_teacher_ratio"
)
context_vars <- intersect(c("id","school_name","state"), names(data))
use_cols <- unique(c(context_vars, intersect(key_vars, names(data))))
df     <- data[, use_cols, drop = FALSE]
num_df <- df[, sapply(df, is.numeric), drop = FALSE]

missing <- setdiff(key_vars, names(df))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  cat("Note: missing expected columns →", paste(missing, collapse = ", "), "\n\n")
}

```

**id** — Unique identifier for each school entry.

**school_name** — Name of the school (synthetically generated).

**state** — U.S. state where the school is located.

**school_type** — Type of institution: Public, Private, or Charter.

**grade_level** — Primary level served by the school: Elementary, Middle, or High.

**funding_per_student_usd** — Annual funding per student in U.S. dollars.

**avg_test_score_percent** — Average student performance score (0–100%).

**student_teacher_ratio** — Average number of students per teacher.

**percent_low_income** — Percentage of students from low-income households.

**percent_minority** — Percentage of students from minority backgrounds.

**internet_access_percent** — Percentage of students with internet access at school.

**dropout_rate_percent** — Annual dropout rate among students (as a percentage)

# Descriptive Statistics 

## Summary of Key Variables
To better understand dropout rates across schools, we first calculated basic descriptive statistics. This step helps us understand tendencies in the data, how spread out the values are, and whether there are any unusual observations.


```{r Summary of Key Variables,results='asis',echo=FALSE}
summary_table <- data.frame(
  Min    = sapply(num_df, \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
  Q1     = sapply(num_df, \(x) quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
  Median = sapply(num_df, \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
  Mean   = sapply(num_df, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
  Q3     = sapply(num_df, \(x) quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)),
  Max    = sapply(num_df, \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
  SD     = sapply(num_df, \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
)
kable(round(summary_table, 2),
      caption = " Descriptive summary for key variables .") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```
The descriptive statistics show several important patterns in the dataset.
School funding per student varies widely, ranging from around $5,000 to $24,000, which indicates large differences in resources across schools. The percentage of low-income students also shows considerable spread (10% to 94%), meaning some schools serve mostly high-income families while others serve predominantly low-income communities.

Student performance indicators follow the same pattern: average test scores range from 40% to 100%, showing strong differences in academic achievement across schools. 

The dropout rate itself ranges from 0.5% to 14.9%, with an average around 7–8%, meaning dropout levels are generally moderate but vary notably between schools. 

Overall, the table highlights clear variability in funding, demographics, and academic performance. 

This variation is important because it gives a strong reason to explore whether these differences help explain changes in dropout rates.

## Distribution of Dropout Rate


```{r Figure 1, fig.cap="Distribution of Dropout Rate", echo=FALSE}
drop <- df$dropout_rate_percent

# mean and sd
mean_drop <- mean(drop, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_drop   <- sd(drop, na.rm = TRUE)

# نحدد نطاق الـ X بشكل يدوي + أوسع من البيانات
x_range <- seq(min(drop) - 5, max(drop) + 5, length = 200)

# نبدأ بالرسم فقط للمحور بدون بيانات
plot(x_range,
     dnorm(x_range, mean_drop, sd_drop),
     type = "l",
     lwd = 3,
     col = "green",
     main = "Dropout Rate Distribution",
     xlab = "Dropout Rate (%)",
     ylab = "Density")

# نضيف الهستوغرام فوق الخط


# نضيف خط يوضح المتوسط
abline(v = mean_drop, col = "black", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

```
  
  
The plot displays a normal density curve representing the distribution of dropout rates, centered around the sample mean (shown by the vertical dashed line). The curve uses the observed mean and standard deviation to approximate how dropout rates are spread across schools. The distribution is roughly symmetric, with most values concentrated near the mean and fewer schools appearing at very low or very high dropout rates. This visualization highlights the typical dropout level in the dataset and shows how individual schools deviate from the average.

# Anlaisys

## Multiple Linear Regression

### Objective

To determine whether the predictor variables
(funding per student, percent low-income, average test score, and student–teacher ratio)
have a statistically significant effect on the dropout rate.

The model will help us identify which factors contribute the most to students dropping out.

### Hypotheses
We want to test whether the predictors (funding per student, % low-income students, average test score, and student-teacher ratio) have an effect on the dropout rate.

**Null Hypothesis (H₀):**

$$
\beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = \beta_4 =\beta_5 = 0
$$

None of the predictors have a significant effect on dropout rate  


**Alternative Hypothesis (H₁):**

$$
\text{At least one } \beta_i \neq 0
$$

At least one predictor has a significant effect on dropout rate.

\newpage
### Formula 

Multiple Linear Regression model:

$$
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_3 + \beta_4 X_4 +\beta_4 X_5+ \epsilon
$$

Where: 

 Y = dropout rate (%) 
 
 X_1 =funding per student 
 
 X_2 =percent low-income 
 
 X_3 =average test score 
 
 X_4 =student-teacher ratio 
 
 X_5=percent_minority

### Multiple Linear Regression Implement
```{r multy r,results='asis',echo=TRUE}
mlr_model <- lm(dropout_rate_percent ~ funding_per_student_usd +
                  percent_low_income +
                  avg_test_score_percent +
                  percent_minority+ 
                  student_teacher_ratio,
                  data = df)


```

```{r tidy-summary, results='asis'}
library(broom)
library(knitr)

tidy_mlr <- tidy(mlr_model)
tidy_mlr$term <- recode(tidy_mlr$term,
   "(Intercept)"              = "Intercept",
   "funding_per_student_usd"  = "Funding per student",
   "percent_low_income"       = "% Low-income students",
   "avg_test_score_percent"   = "Average test score",
   "percent_minority"         = "% Minority students",
   "student_teacher_ratio"    = "Student–teacher ratio"
)
kable(tidy_mlr,
      caption = "Summary of Multiple Linear Regression Model",
      digits = 4)
```
### ANOVA Table
```{r anova ,echo=FALSE}

library(broom)
library(knitr)

tidy_mlr <- tidy(anova(mlr_model))
tidy_mlr$term <- recode(tidy_mlr$term,
   "(Intercept)"              = "Intercept",
   "funding_per_student_usd"  = "Funding per student",
   "percent_low_income"       = "% Low-income students",
   "avg_test_score_percent"   = "Average test score",
   "percent_minority"         = "% Minority students",
   "student_teacher_ratio"    = "Student–teacher ratio"
)
kable(tidy_mlr,
      caption = "Summary of ANOVA Table",
      digits = 4)
```

### Decision Rule

At significance level α = 0.05:

 • If p-value < 0.05 → Reject H_0
 
→ At least one predictor significantly affects dropout rate.

 • If p-value ≥ 0.05 → Fail to reject H_0
 
→ Predictors do not have meaningful influence.

\newpage

### Interpretation

The multiple linear regression model examined whether the following variables:

- Funding per student (USD)
- Percentage of low-income students
- Average test score (percent)
- Student–teacher ratio
- Percentage of Minority students

can predict the dropout rate (%) in schools.

Based on the regression output:

| Predictor                | p-value | Result                    |
|--------------------------|---------|---------------------------|
| Funding per student      | 0.217   | Not statistically significant |
| % Low-income students    | 0.916   | Not statistically significant |
| Average test score       | 0.561   | Not statistically significant |
| Student–teacher ratio    | 0.673   | Not statistically significant |
| % Minority students      | 0.935   | Not statistically significant |

The multiple linear regression results show that the model has a very weak
ability to explain dropout rates. The R² value is extremely small (0.0021),
meaning the predictors together explain only 0.21% of the variation in
dropout rate. This indicates that the overall relationship between the
predictor variables and dropout rate is very weak.

Additionally, all predictor variables have high p-values, showing that none
of them have a statistically significant effect on dropout rate. The
negative adjusted R² further supports that the model does not improve the
prediction beyond using the mean alone.

In simple terms, the variables included in the model (funding per student,
percent low-income, average test score, and student-teacher ratio) do not
meaningfully predict dropout rate in this dataset. This suggests that other
factors — possibly behavioral, social, or school-environment factors — may
have a stronger influence on dropout levels.



## Simple Linear Regression
### Objective
The objective of the simple linear regression is to examine whether one predictor variable (e.g., funding per student, percent low-income, test score, or student–teacher ratio) has a significant linear relationship with the dropout rate (%).
This helps us understand the effect of each variable separately before building the full multiple regression model.


### Hypotheses

**Null Hypothesis (H₀):**

$$
\beta_1 = 0
$$
There is no linear relationship between the predictor and dropout rate.


**Alternative Hypothesis (H₁):**

$$
 \beta_i \neq 0
$$
The predictor does have a significant linear effect on dropout rate.

\newpage

### Formula 

Simple Linear Regression model:

$$
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1  + \epsilon
$$

Where: 

 Y = dropout rate (%) 
 
 X_1 =one predictor 
 
 \beta_0 = intercept
 
 \beta_1 = slope (effect of the predictor on dropout rate)
 
 \varepsilon = random error term



```{r s lm, results='asis',echo=TRUE}
# Simple models: one predictor at a time
m_funding  <- lm(dropout_rate_percent ~ funding_per_student_usd, data = df)
m_lowinc   <- lm(dropout_rate_percent ~ percent_low_income,      data = df)
m_tests    <- lm(dropout_rate_percent ~ avg_test_score_percent,  data = df)
m_minority <- lm(dropout_rate_percent ~ percent_minority,        data = df)
m_ratio    <- lm(dropout_rate_percent ~ student_teacher_ratio,   data = df)
```



```{r , results='asis' ,echo=FALSE}
library(broom)
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

simple_models <- list(
  Funding        = m_funding,
  Low_income     = m_lowinc,
  Test_score     = m_tests,
  Minority       = m_minority,
  Student_teacher= m_ratio
)

simple_summary <- lapply(names(simple_models), function(name) {
  g <- glance(simple_models[[name]])
  data.frame(
    Predictor = name,
    R2        = round(g$r.squared, 4),
    p_value   = round(g$p.value, 4)
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

kable(simple_summary,
      caption = "Simple linear regression models: dropout rate vs. each predictor")
```

\newpage

### Decision Rule

At significance level α = 0.05:

• If p-value < 0.05 → Reject H_0: predictor have a linear relationship with the dropout rate

• If p-value ≥ 0.05 → Fail to reject H_0: predictor does not have a linear relationship with the dropout rate



### Interpretation
The simple linear regression models examined whether each predictor, taken one at a time, can explain the dropout rate (%) in schools.

The predictors we tested are:
- Funding per student (USD)  
- Percentage of low-income students  
- Average test score (percent)  
- Percentage of minority students  
- Student–teacher ratio  

Based on the simple regression outputs, we summarize the results in the following table:

| Predictor              | R²      | p-value | Result                     |
|------------------------|---------|--------:|----------------------------|
| Funding per student    | 0.0016  | 0.2071  | does not have linear relationship with the dropout rate |
| % Low-income students  | 0.0000  | 0.9505  | does not have linear relationship with the dropout rate |
| Average test score     | 0.0004  | 0.5545  | does not have linear relationship with the dropout rate |
| % Minority students    | 0.0000  | 0.9444  | does not have linear relationship with the dropout rate |
| Student–teacher ratio  | 0.0002  | 0.6667  | does not have llinear relationship with the dropout rate |

At a significance level of 0.05, all p-values are greater than 0.05, so none of the predictors show a statistically linear relationship with dropout rate when tested alone.  

The R² values are also very small (all close to 0), which means that each simple model explains almost none of the variation in dropout rate. In simple words, looking at only one factor at a time (funding, low-income %, test score, minority %, or teacher ratio) does not help us predict dropout rate well in this dataset.

\newpage





  

       
## Correlation matrix

The correlation matrix examines how strongly each variable is related to the dropout rate and to one another. The values range from –1 to +1, where numbers close to 0 indicate very weak or no linear relationship.
```{r , results='asis' ,echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# أسماء جديدة قصيرة
names_for_table <- c("% Dropout", "Funding", "% Low-income",
                     "% Minority", "% Test Score", "Student Teacher Ratio")

# المتغيرات الأصلية
num_vars <- df[, c("dropout_rate_percent",
                   "funding_per_student_usd",
                   "percent_low_income",
                   "percent_minority",
                   "avg_test_score_percent",
                   "student_teacher_ratio")]

# مصفوفة الارتباط
cor_mat <- cor(num_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# إعادة تسمية الصفوف + الأعمدة بدون تغيير البيانات الأصلية
colnames(cor_mat) <- names_for_table
rownames(cor_mat) <- names_for_table

# طباعة الجدول بشكل جميل
kable(round(cor_mat, 3),
      caption = "Correlation Matrix of Key Variables")

``` 

Relationship with Dropout Rate

 • Funding per student (r = –0.040)
 
→ Almost no relationship. Higher funding does not appear to reduce dropout rates.

 • % Low-income students (r = 0.002)
 
→ No relationship. The proportion of low-income students does not show a meaningful pattern with dropout rate.

 • % Minority students (r = –0.002)
 
→ No relationship. Schools with higher minority percentages do not show higher or lower dropout rates.

 • Average test score (r = –0.019)
 
→ Very weak negative relationship, almost zero. Higher test scores do not meaningfully predict dropout.

 • Student–teacher ratio (r = 0.014)
 
→ No relationship. Class size differences do not explain dropout variation.


All correlations with dropout rate are extremely weak (near 0), meaning no single variable shows a strong linear relationship with dropout rate.

\newpage
# Conclusion
Overall, this project provided a clear statistical overview of the factors that might influence the dropout rate (%) in U.S. public schools. The descriptive statistics and visualizations—such as histograms and boxplots—showed that schools differ widely in funding levels, socioeconomic composition, average test scores, and student–teacher ratios. These plots highlighted broad distributions, moderate variability across schools, and differences in school contexts.

When examining linear relationships, the correlation matrix revealed that dropout rate has extremely weak correlations (close to zero) with all predictors. None of the variables—funding per student, low-income percentage, minority percentage, average test score, or student–teacher ratio—showed meaningful linear association with dropout rate.

The simple linear regression models confirmed this pattern: each predictor individually had a very low R² and non-significant p-values, meaning no single variable provides useful predictive power.

Finally, the multiple linear regression model also showed:

 • No significant predictors
 
 • Very low R² (≈ 0.002)
 
 • Negative adjusted R², indicating the model performs worse than simply using the mean dropout rate
 
 • High p-values for all variables, including % minority, showing no statistical evidence that these factors explain dropout variation
 

In simple terms, the variables included in this dataset do not meaningfully predict dropout rates. This suggests that dropout levels may be influenced by factors not captured here, such as behavioral challenges, school climate, family environment, mental health support, community factors, or attendance issues.

In conclusion, while the dataset provides valuable insights into school characteristics, it does not explain why dropout rates differ between schools. Future studies should incorporate more detailed, student-level, or behavioral variables to better understand what truly drives student dropout and support more effective educational interventions.
